t: 3644. Maximum K to Sort a Permutation — Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem
Swaps of indices i, j are allowed only when nums[i] AND nums[j] == k, for one global k we choose. Maximize k while keeping the array sortable. Only positions where nums[i] ≠ i matter — sorted positions never need to participate. In examples, the answer equals the AND of all values sitting at wrong positions: {3,1}→1, {3,2}→2, {3,2,1,0}→0.

Why necessary: every misplaced value must eventually move, and the final swap that places value v joins v with some partner under AND == k, forcing k's bits into v. Why sufficient: with k = AND of all misplaced values, the misplaced values form a connected swap structure allowing a sorting sequence.
k: Ignore indices already holding the correct value.
Answer k = bitwise AND of nums[i] over all i with nums[i] ≠ i (0 if already sorted).
Necessity follows from the last swap touching each misplaced value; sufficiency from constructing swaps within the misplaced-value subgraph.

a.i: Scan once, folding AND over values at incorrect positions. Already-correct positions contribute nothing. Runs in O(n) with O(1) space.
s: For each i with nums[i] != i: k = nums[i] if unset else k & nums[i].
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant-time fold.

w: This one-liner fold is the whole problem once the invariant is spotted; prove necessity in interviews before coding. Pitfalls: returning -1 sentinel instead of 0 for a sorted array, and including correct positions in the AND (which can wrongly shrink k). Follow-up: minimum number of allowed swaps to sort, or the case where k may vary per swap.
